theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: Which of these is a project rather than routine operations?
options: Checking in guests at a hotel's front desk each day
Paying staff salaries at the end of every single month
Cleaning the guest rooms in a hotel every morning
Refurbishing a hotel's restaurant within six months

questions.stem: A project manager is told the deadline for a new booking website has moved forward by a month. What else is most likely to be affected?
options: The number of public holidays in the year
The cost, the scope or the quality of the work
The company's yearly tax return and its audit
The prices charged on competitors' websites

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of a project charter (or initiation document)?
options: To authorise the project and set out its aims, scope and sponsor
To list every task in the project and the hours each will take
To record the minutes of each weekly project team meeting
To show the final accounts once the project has been closed

questions.stem: On a project to build a visitor centre at a heritage site, who is the project sponsor?
options: The contractor who builds the centre on the site
The newest member of the project's working team
The senior person who owns the business case and funding
A visitor who has written in asking for the centre

questions.stem: A tour company plans a new river rafting excursion in Portland. Which step should come early in the planning?
options: Print the brochures and posters for the new excursion
Buy the rafts and equipment at the lowest price found
Find out who it affects, such as residents and guides

questions.stem: Why should a project's scope be written down and agreed at the start?
options: So everyone knows what is included and what is not
So the project manager can add work freely later on
So the sponsor need not approve any later changes
So the budget can be left until the work has begun

questions.stem: During a hotel lobby upgrade, the general manager keeps asking the team to add small extra jobs without changing the budget or the date. What is this called?
options: Critical path
Risk transfer
Fast tracking
Scope creep

questions.stem: A stakeholder asks for a major new feature in a ministry's online licensing system halfway through the project. What should the project manager do?
options: Add it at once to keep the stakeholder happy with the project
Assess its effect on time, cost and risk, then seek approval

options: The project's work divided into smaller parts to manage
The organisation's reporting lines and all its job titles

questions.stem: In a festival project, the stage cannot be built until the site has been cleared. What kind of link is this between the two tasks?
options: A milestone
A work package
A lag

options: 14 days
12 days
9 days
10 days

options: 5 days
2 days
3 days

questions.stem: Why does a project manager pay close attention to the critical path?
options: It shows which tasks in the project cost the least
A delay to any task on it delays the whole project
It lists the tasks to skip if time becomes short
It shows the tasks that the sponsor likes best

questions.stem: What does a network (precedence) diagram mainly show about a project's tasks?
options: The order of tasks and how they depend on each other
The cost of each task as a share of the whole budget
The names and phone numbers of each of the suppliers
The reporting lines between the project's managers

A cost that was not included in the original budget
A team member who has left the project early

options: 6 days
8 days
7 days
9 days

questions.stem: Which is the most reliable basis for estimating the cost of a hotel's new swimming pool?
options: Written quotes from qualified contractors for the agreed design
The cost of a pool the manager saw while on holiday abroad
A guess made by the general manager at a staff meeting
The amount left over in this year's maintenance budget

options: Leave both tasks in place and hope that it works out
Move one task to a free week, or find another electrician

The salaries and allowances of the project team members

options: Transfer
Avoid

So the sponsor need never read the register at all

options: A risk might happen; an issue has already happened

questions.stem: A weekly status report shows a project's budget as 'amber'. What does this usually mean?
options: The budget has been fully spent and the account closed
The budget is on track and there are no concerns at all

questions.stem: A project has an earned value of J$1,800,000 and an actual cost of J$2,000,000. What is its cost performance index (CPI), and what does it mean?
options: 1.11: it is under budget
0.90: it is ahead of schedule
1.11: it is behind schedule
0.90: it is over budget

questions.stem: A project's planned value to date is J$2,400,000 and its earned value is J$1,800,000. What is its schedule performance index (SPI)?
Which is the most reliable way to track progress on a project?
options: Ask the team each week whether they feel things are going well
Compare work done, cost and dates against the approved plan
Count the hours the project manager spends in the office
Wait until the very end to see whether the deadline was met

questions.stem: A building task is two weeks behind and is on the critical path. Which is a sensible option to recover the time?
options: Remove the task from the plan altogether and carry on as before
Move the project's end date without telling anyone
Stop reporting progress until the task is finished

questions.stem: How should quality be managed on a project to install a new hotel booking system?
options: Agree acceptance criteria and test before it goes live
Let the supplier decide when the system is good enough

questions.stem: A public body's project needs a contractor for J$25,000,000 of building work. What must the project manager make sure of?
options: The contract goes to the first contractor who telephones

questions.stem: A project team has members from sales, IT and operations who report to different managers. What should the project manager do early on?
options: Agree roles and time commitments with them and their managers
Let each member decide their own tasks and their deadlines
Ask each of their managers to attend every team meeting
Hold all project meetings without telling their managers

questions.stem: Two team members disagree about the best design for a resort's new spa. What should the project manager do?
options: Choose the idea put forward by the more senior team member
Bring them together to weigh the options against the aims
Tell them both to stop discussing it and to carry on
Remove both of them from the project team at once

questions.stem: A local community group strongly opposes a new attraction near its village and has the ear of the municipal corporation. How should the project manager treat this group?
options: Ignore it, as it has no formal role in the project
Send it a copy of the final report when work is done
Manage it closely: consult, listen and keep it informed
Ask the police to keep its members out of meetings

questions.stem: A project to build cabins near a beach in St Elizabeth must get permits before work starts. What should the project plan include?
options: A decision to start building and apply for permits later
A plan to build the cabins without telling the authorities
Only the cost of the cabins and not the cost of permits
Time and tasks for planning and environmental approvals

questions.stem: During site work at a resort, guests are walking close to an area where a crane is lifting. What should the project manager do?
options: Ask the guests to watch their step as they pass the crane
Let the lifting continue, as the guests are all adults
Stop the lift and fence off the area with clear signs
Put a note about it in the next weekly status report

questions.stem: Which activity belongs in closing a project?
options: Handing over, getting sign-off and releasing resources
Writing the project charter and naming the sponsor
Breaking the scope down into a work breakdown structure
Estimating task times using the three-point method

questions.stem: Why is a lessons-learned review held at the end of a project?
options: To decide which member of the team should be blamed
To record what went well and badly for future projects
To change the original aims so that they look as if met
To collect the team's views on the sponsor's character

questions.stem: Six months after a new online booking system went live, the hotel checks whether bookings and costs improved as planned. What is this review called?
options: A risk assessment
A kick-off meeting
A stage gate review meeting
A benefits realisation review

questions.stem: Which order shows the usual phases of a project?
options: Planning, closing, initiation, then execution and control
Initiation, planning, execution and control, then closing
Execution and control, initiation, planning, then closing
Closing, planning, execution and control, then initiation

questions.stem: A project has spent J$4,200,000 of its J$6,000,000 budget, but only 60% of the work is done. What should the project manager conclude?
options: The project is well under budget at this point
The project is exactly on budget at this point

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of a project kick-off meeting?
options: To approve the final payments due to all of the suppliers
To close the project and release the team to other work
To decide whether or not the project should exist at all
To share the plan, roles and ways of working with the team

questions.stem: Why might a project manager use project management software for a large hotel renovation?
options: To schedule tasks, track progress and share updates in one place
To replace all meetings with the project team and the sponsor
To make decisions on the project's scope without asking the sponsor
To avoid having to keep a risk register for the project at all

questions.stem: Before a project to open a new tour route is approved, what should the business case show?
options: The costs, benefits, risks and options, with a recommendation
Only the colour scheme for the tour buses and staff uniforms

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What is the name of the chart that shows project tasks as horizontal bars against a timeline?
Tasks P (4 days), Q (6 days) and R (3 days) must be done one after another. Task S (5 days) starts after P and must finish before R, alongside Q. How many days long is the critical path?
What two-word term names the link between time, cost and scope in a project, where changing one affects the others?
What word names a product or result that a project must hand over, such as a finished report or a built cabin?
What word names any person or group affected by a project, or able to affect it?
What word names the approved version of the schedule and budget against which progress is measured?
A task's optimistic time is 2 days, its most likely time is 5 days and its pessimistic time is 14 days. Using the three-point (PERT) formula, what is the expected time, in days?
A project's earned value is J$3,000,000 and its actual cost is J$2,500,000. What is its cost performance index (CPI)?
A project's cost estimate is J$8,000,000, and a 5% contingency is added. How much is the contingency, in J$?
What two-word term names the record of problems that have already arisen on a project, with their owners and actions?
What one word names the time a task can be delayed without delaying the project's end date?
Give the three-letter abbreviation for the colour code in status reports that shows whether an item is on track, at risk or in trouble.
A project's planned value to date is J$5,000,000 and its earned value is J$4,000,000. What is its schedule performance index (SPI)?
What is the usual name for the final document that records what a project delivered against its aims, cost and time?
A project has 40 tasks of equal size, and 26 of them are done. What percentage of the project is complete?

essays.stem: A hotel in Ocho Rios plans to refurbish its 40-room east wing between May and October while staying open to guests. Describe how you would plan the project.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start with a project charter agreed with the general manager as sponsor: the aims, such as all 40 rooms refurbished to the new standard by 31 October within J$60,000,000, the scope, including what is not included, and the main constraints, such as keeping guest disruption low. I would identify stakeholders: guests, staff, owners, contractors, suppliers and the parish authorities for any permits. Next I would break the work into a work breakdown structure: design, permits, procurement, strip-out, building work, finishes, furniture, inspection and handover. I would estimate each task from contractors' quotes and past jobs, link the tasks and build a Gantt chart, finding the critical path. I would phase the work in blocks of ten rooms so the rest of the hotel stays open, and schedule noisy work for weekday daytime. The budget would include a contingency. I would set up a risk register covering hurricanes, late deliveries, guest complaints and safety, a communication plan for guests and staff, quality checks for each room and a weekly progress meeting.
markingPoints: Sets out aims, scope and constraints in a charter with the sponsor
Identifies stakeholders, including guests, staff and authorities
Breaks down the work, estimates it and builds a schedule with a critical path
Plans phasing to keep the hotel open, with a budget and contingency
Plans risk, communication, quality and progress control

essays.stem: Using a three-day food and music festival as an example, explain how you would build a project schedule with a work breakdown structure, dependencies, a Gantt chart and the critical path.
essays.modelAnswer: I would first break the festival into main parts in a work breakdown structure: site and permits, artists and programme, vendors, marketing and tickets, staffing and security, and closing and clean-up. Each part would be divided into tasks small enough to estimate and assign, such as 'book the main stage' or 'get the noise permit'. I would estimate each task's duration, using quotes, past festivals and three-point estimates for uncertain tasks. Next I would set the dependencies: for example, tickets cannot go on sale until the main artists are confirmed, and the stage cannot be built until the site is cleared and the permit granted. I would draw these links in a network diagram and work forwards to find the earliest finish date, which shows the critical path: the longest chain, here likely permits, site preparation, stage build and sound checks. Tasks off that path have float. I would then put the tasks on a Gantt chart with milestones, such as 'artists confirmed', assign owners and check that resources are not double-booked. The approved chart would become the baseline.
markingPoints: Breaks the festival into a work breakdown structure and tasks
Estimates durations using quotes, history or three-point estimates
Sets dependencies with sensible examples
Finds the critical path and float
Builds a Gantt chart with milestones, owners and a baseline

essays.stem: Describe how you would identify, assess and manage the risks on a project to open a new nature tour in the Cockpit Country.
essays.modelAnswer: I would identify risks by holding a workshop with the team, guides, community members and an environmental adviser, and by checking lessons from similar tours. Risks might include visitor injury on rough trails, heavy rain and landslides, damage to the forest, objection from local residents, delays in getting permits, a key guide leaving and fewer bookings than forecast. I would enter each in a risk register and score its likelihood and impact on a 1 to 5 scale, multiplying them to rank the risks. For each serious risk I would choose a response: reduce it, for example by training guides in first aid and setting weather rules for cancelling tours; avoid it, by keeping groups off sensitive areas; transfer it, through insurance and clear booking terms; or accept small risks with a contingency. Each risk would have an owner, actions and a date. I would also involve the community early and share benefits, such as local guiding jobs. The register would be reviewed at every weekly meeting, and serious changes reported to the sponsor.
markingPoints: Identifies risks with the team and stakeholders, with suitable examples
Records them in a register and scores likelihood and impact
Chooses suitable responses: reduce, avoid, transfer or accept
Names owners and actions, including community involvement
Reviews the register regularly and reports serious changes

essays.stem: A project's monthly report shows a cost performance index (CPI) of 0.85 and a schedule performance index (SPI) of 1.05. Explain what these figures mean and what the project manager should do.
essays.modelAnswer: A CPI of 0.85 means that for every J$1 spent, only about 85 cents' worth of planned work has been done, so the project is over budget. If this continues, the final cost will be well above the budget; for example, a J$10,000,000 budget would end at about J$11,800,000. An SPI of 1.05 means the work done is slightly ahead of the work planned to date, so the project is a little ahead of schedule. Together, the figures may mean the team is spending more to move faster, such as through overtime or extra contractors, or that some costs are higher than estimated. The project manager should first check that the figures are correct, then find which tasks are causing the overspend. Possible actions include reducing overtime now that the schedule is ahead, renegotiating supplier prices, finding cheaper ways to deliver the remaining work or, if needed, asking the sponsor to approve a change in budget or scope. The manager should report the position honestly, with a new forecast and the recovery plan, and watch the trend over the following months.
markingPoints: Explains that CPI 0.85 means the project is over budget
Explains that SPI 1.05 means it is slightly ahead of schedule
Links the two, such as spending more to move faster
Checks the data and finds the cause by task
Proposes corrective actions, a new forecast and honest reporting

essays.stem: A community tourism project in a fishing village in St Thomas involves residents, fishers, the municipal corporation, a funding agency and tour operators. Explain how you would manage these stakeholders.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start by listing all stakeholders and what each wants from the project and fears about it. Residents may want jobs and less disruption; fishers may worry about losing beach access; the municipal corporation cares about permits and public good; the funding agency wants results and proper use of money; tour operators want a reliable product to sell. I would map them by their power and interest. The funding agency and municipal corporation, with high power, need close management, regular reports and early involvement in decisions. Residents and fishers, with high interest, need to be consulted through community meetings and a liaison group, and their concerns built into the plan, such as protecting landing sites. Tour operators should be kept informed and asked for feedback on the product. I would agree a communication plan covering who gets what information, how often and through which channels, including meetings in the village, WhatsApp updates and written reports. I would record concerns and responses, and review the stakeholder map as the project changes.
markingPoints: Identifies each stakeholder's interests and concerns
Maps stakeholders by power and interest
Chooses suitable approaches for each group, such as close management or consultation
Sets a communication plan with methods and frequency
Records concerns and reviews the map over time

essays.stem: Explain how a project manager should control changes to a project's scope, and why this matters.
essays.modelAnswer: Changes are normal in projects, but uncontrolled changes, known as scope creep, are a common cause of late and over-budget projects. The project manager should agree the scope in writing at the start, with clear deliverables and exclusions, and set up a change control process. Anyone who wants a change submits a change request describing what they want and why. The project manager, with the team, assesses the effect on time, cost, quality, resources and risk, and on other tasks through the dependencies. The request then goes to the sponsor or a change board, who approve, reject or defer it. If approved, the plan, budget, schedule and baseline are updated, the team is told and the change is recorded in a change log. Small changes may be approved by the project manager within agreed limits. This matters because it keeps decisions with the right people, protects the budget and deadline, makes the cost of each change clear, and gives a record if the project is later reviewed.
markingPoints: Explains scope creep and its effects
Agrees the scope in writing at the start
Uses change requests and assesses effect on time, cost, quality and risk
Gets approval from the sponsor or change board and updates the plan and log
Explains why control matters for budget, time and accountability

essays.stem: Describe how you would lead a project team made up of staff from different departments who still report to their own line managers.
essays.modelAnswer: Because I would not be the team members' line manager, I would rely on agreement and influence rather than authority. At the start I would meet each line manager to agree how much of each person's time the project needs and for how long, and confirm it in writing. I would hold a kick-off meeting to explain the project's aims, the plan and why it matters, and agree roles using a RACI chart so that everyone knows who is responsible, who decides and who is consulted. We would agree ways of working, such as meeting times, how decisions are made and how to raise problems. I would plan tasks around their other duties where possible. During the project I would hold short weekly progress meetings, recognise good work, and tell line managers about their staff's contribution, which also feeds into their appraisals. When conflicts come up, between team members or with departmental work, I would deal with them early and openly, using the project's aims as the guide, and go to the sponsor if a resource conflict cannot be settled.
markingPoints: Agrees time commitments with line managers
Explains aims and agrees roles, for example with a RACI chart
Agrees ways of working and plans around other duties
Motivates through progress meetings, recognition and feedback to line managers
Handles conflicts early and escalates resource conflicts to the sponsor

essays.stem: Compare a traditional, step-by-step ('waterfall') approach with an agile, iterative approach for building a tour company's new online booking website, and recommend one.
essays.modelAnswer: In a waterfall approach, all the requirements are fixed at the start, then design, building, testing and launch follow in order. It gives a clear scope, budget and end date, which suits fixed contracts and makes reporting simple. However, if the business's needs change or the first design proves wrong, changes are costly, and users may not see the website until near the end. In an agile approach, the work is done in short cycles, often two weeks, each producing a working part of the website that users test. Priorities are reviewed after each cycle, so the website can change as the business learns what customers need. It needs a business owner who is available to make decisions regularly, and the final scope and cost are less certain at the start. For a booking website, where customer needs and online payment options may change and early feedback is valuable, I would recommend an agile approach, with a fixed budget and launch date, a prioritised list of features and a working basic booking function delivered first.
markingPoints: Describes the waterfall approach with its strengths
Notes the weaknesses of waterfall when needs change
Describes the agile approach with its strengths
Notes what agile needs and its uncertainties
Makes a justified recommendation for this project

essays.stem: Explain how you would close a project and evaluate its success.
essays.modelAnswer: I would first confirm that every deliverable is complete and meets the agreed acceptance criteria, then hand it over to the people who will run it, with training, manuals and warranties, and get formal sign-off from the sponsor. I would close all contracts, check the final invoices against the work done and settle any claims. The project accounts would be closed and the final cost compared with the budget. Team members would be released back to their departments, with thanks and feedback to their line managers. I would then hold a lessons-learned review with the team and key stakeholders, looking at what went well, what went badly and why, covering planning, estimating, risks, communication and suppliers. To evaluate success, I would compare the results with the aims in the charter: was the scope delivered, on time, within budget and to quality, and were stakeholders satisfied? I would write a closure report with these findings and recommendations and store the files. Later, a benefits review would check whether the expected benefits, such as more bookings, were achieved.
markingPoints: Confirms deliverables meet acceptance criteria and gets sign-off
Hands over with training and documents
Closes contracts and accounts and releases the team
Holds a lessons-learned review
Evaluates results against aims in a closure report, with a later benefits review

essays.stem: A government agency's project needs an outside contractor to install a new visitor information system at three sites. Explain how the project manager should manage procurement and the contractor.
essays.modelAnswer: The project manager should first work with the agency's procurement unit, because public bodies must follow the procurement rules for public bodies, which aim at fairness, competition, transparency and value for money. A clear specification would be written, setting out what the system must do, the sites, the timeline, the acceptance tests and the warranty and support needed. The procurement method would be chosen to suit the value, and bids judged against criteria set out in advance, such as price, experience, technical quality and support. Anyone with a conflict of interest must declare it and step away. The contract would include the scope, price and payment stages linked to milestones, delivery dates, penalties or remedies for delay, and data protection terms. Once work begins, the project manager would hold regular progress meetings with the contractor, check work against the specification, keep records, and manage any changes through the agreed change process. Payments would be made only for accepted work. At the end, the system would be tested and accepted at each site before final payment, and the contractor's performance recorded.
markingPoints: Works with procurement and follows the public procurement rules
Writes a clear specification with acceptance tests
Uses fair, pre-set evaluation criteria and manages conflicts of interest
Includes key contract terms such as milestones, payment stages and remedies
Monitors the contractor, manages changes and pays only for accepted work

practical1.title: Plan a small project: charter, work breakdown, Gantt chart, budget and risk register
practical1.brief: The assessor gives your group a brief for a small made-up project, for example setting up a heritage walking tour in Falmouth, opening a small coffee kiosk at a craft market or running a one-day community tourism fair, with a budget limit, a deadline and a list of tasks with rough durations and costs. As a group, prepare the project plan. Give each member a named role: project manager (writes the one-page project charter with aims, scope, exclusions, sponsor and constraints), planner (builds the work breakdown structure and sets the dependencies), scheduler (draws the Gantt chart in a spreadsheet or project software, marks the critical path and milestones, and works out the float), budget officer (builds the budget with a contingency, checking every figure twice), and risk officer (writes a risk register with scores, responses, owners and actions). In a group of four, the project manager also writes the risk register. Finish with a 10-minute presentation of the plan to the assessor as sponsor.
materials: Project brief with tasks, durations and costs from the assessor
Computers with spreadsheet or project software
Flipchart paper, markers and sticky notes
photos: The work breakdown structure on flipchart or screen
The Gantt chart with the critical path and milestones marked
The group presenting the plan to the sponsor
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the plan
Charter states clear aims, scope, exclusions and constraints
Work breakdown covers all the work and dependencies are sensible
Critical path and project duration are correct
Budget adds up, includes a contingency and stays within the limit
Risk register scores risks and gives responses and owners
Presented clearly and answered the sponsor's questions
safety: Treat the brief as confidential; return printouts to the assessor
Use made-up names for people and suppliers
Respect each other's ideas and share the workload fairly
Take a short break away from the screen during the task

practical2.title: Run a mid-project review: measure progress, handle a change request and report to the sponsor
practical2.brief: The assessor gives your group a status pack for a made-up project halfway through, for example a hotel booking system upgrade or a museum refit: the baseline Gantt chart and budget, progress to date, actual costs, an issue list and a change request from a stakeholder. As a group, review the project and report to the sponsor. Give each member a named role: analyst (works out planned value, earned value, CPI and SPI and a forecast final cost in a spreadsheet, checking every figure twice), scheduler (updates the Gantt chart with actual progress and shows the effect on the end date), change assessor (assesses the change request for its effect on time, cost, quality and risk and makes a recommendation), issues lead (updates the issue log with owners and actions), and project manager (writes a one-page status report with RAG ratings and leads a 15-minute review meeting with the assessor playing the sponsor). In a group of four, the project manager also updates the issue log.
materials: Project status pack from the assessor
Computers with spreadsheet or project software
photos: The spreadsheet on screen with planned value, earned value, CPI, SPI and the forecast
The updated Gantt chart showing progress and the new end date
The change request assessment and recommendation
The status report with RAG ratings and the review meeting in progress
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the evidence
CPI, SPI and the forecast final cost are correct and were checked twice
Updated Gantt chart correctly shows progress and the effect on the end date
Change assessment covers time, cost, quality and risk with a clear recommendation
Status report is honest, clear and uses RAG ratings correctly
Explained the position and options clearly to the sponsor
safety: Treat the project data as confidential business information
